wineFiningCasein.text: A milk protein used to clean up white wine: it binds the polyphenols that make wine brown and bitter, clumps, and sinks. It is racked off with the lees, so little or none should remain.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

butterSculpture.text: Butter shaped into figures. The earliest documented one is from a papal banquet in 1536; American dairy promoters made butter sculptures to compete with margarine from 1890 to 1930, and the Iowa State Fair has shown a butter cow every year since 1911. In Tibetan Buddhism coloured butter torma are altar offerings and lamps burn butter.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

litmusMilk.text: Skim milk with the dye litmus, kept in tubes to see what a bacterium does to milk: sours the lactose, clots or digests the casein, or bleaches the dye. It has been a classroom and diagnostic medium for identifying species for a century.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

skimMilkAgar.text: Skim milk with agar (and nutrients such as tryptone, yeast extract and dextrose) set as a solid plate. The casein makes it opaque, so a bacterium that digests casein with a protease leaves a clear halo around its colonies. A separate lab test medium, not litmus milk.

sources.text: Written from this source.

milkSpray.text: Fresh milk diluted with water and sprayed on squash or zucchini leaves to hold back powdery mildew. In Brazilian greenhouse tests it worked as well as the fungicides fenarimol and benomyl, which is why organic growers use it.

links.name: ECHO, milk as a fungicide (summarising Bettiol, Crop Protection 18, 1999)

sources.text: Written from this source.

caseinCoating.text: Dissolved casein used as the glue in a coating: with clay on art paper in the late 19th to mid 20th century, and with pigment on leather, which is then glazed under heat and pressure. It was the main leather binder by 1920.

sources.text: Written from this source.

flavouredMilk.text: Milk sweetened and flavoured, most often with cocoa, but also with coffee, malt, vanilla, strawberry or banana. It is sold pasteurised and chilled, or UHT-treated and shelf-stable.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

milkTea.text: A family of drinks that combine tea and milk, hot or cold, often with spices or sweetener. Some are brewed in milk, others have milk added to strong tea.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

creamLiqueur.text: A liqueur made from dairy cream and a flavoured spirit: whiskey in Irish cream, marula-fruit spirit in Amarula, rum in several others. It can be drunk neat, on ice or in cocktails.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

milkshake.text: A cold, thick, sweet drink made by blending milk and ice cream with flavourings such as chocolate, caramel, malt or fruit.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

cheesePowder.text: Cheese melted with water and emulsifying salts into a smooth liquid and spray-dried to a powder. It goes into sauces, biscuits, dressings, snack seasonings and the packet in boxed macaroni and cheese; one cheese or several can be used, and the mix sets how much fat and protein it has.

links.name: Felix da Silva et al., Powder Technology 378 (2021)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Kalvdans.text: Kalvdans is a classical Scandinavian dessert. It is made from unpasteurized colostrum milk, the first milk produced by a cow after giving birth.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ábrystir.text: Icelandic colostrum pudding: the first milk after a cow calves, often mixed half and half with whole milk, heated gently over simmering water until it sets firm. Eaten hot or cold, often with cinnamon sugar.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Kharvas.text: Kharvas, also known as Junnu, or Ginnu, is an Indian milk pudding made from cow or buffalo colostrum, the first form of milk produced within one or two days of giving birth. It is prepared by steaming a mix of colostrum, milk, and jaggery or sugar until it coagulates into a jiggling solid. Cardamom, saffron, nutmeg or sesame is added for flavoring. The dish is rich in protein.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

ATryn.text: ATryn is the brand name of the anticoagulant antithrombin manufactured by the Massachusetts-based U.S. company rEVO Biologics. It is made from the milk of goats that have been genetically modified to produce human antithrombin, a plasma protein with anticoagulant properties. Microinjection was used to insert human antithrombin genes into the cell nucleus of their embryos. ATryn is the first medicine produced using genetically engineered animals. GTC states that one genetically modified goat can produce the same amount of antithrombin in a year as 90,000 blood donations. GTC chose goats for the process because they reproduce more rapidly than cattle and produce more protein than rabbits or mice. It has since been withdrawn from the market.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ruconest.text: Conestat alfa, a recombinant human C1-esterase inhibitor taken from the milk of rabbits given the human gene. It was approved in the EU in 2010 and is injected to treat acute attacks of hereditary angioedema. Because it contains traces of rabbit protein, it must not be given to people allergic to rabbits.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Cornish clotted cream.text: Clotted cream made in Cornwall from Cornish milk, a protected designation of origin: at least 55 % fat, cream to golden yellow, with a thick crust formed by scalding. Eaten with jam on scones in a cream tea.

links.name: UK PDO product specification, Cornish Clotted Cream (Defra)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Kaymak.text: Kaymak, also known as qishta or sarshir, is a creamy dairy food similar to clotted cream, made from the milk of water buffalo, cows, sheep, or goats in Central Asia, most Turkic regions on the Eurasian Steppe, the Caucasus, Turkey, most Balkan countries, the Levant, Iran and Iraq.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Malai.text: Malai is a type of clotted cream, originating from the Indian subcontinent. It is used in the cuisine of the Indian subcontinent, especially in sweets from the Indian subcontinent. It is made by heating non-homogenized whole milk to about 80 °C (180 °F) for about one hour and then cooling it. A thick yellowish layer of fat and coagulated proteins forms on the surface, which is skimmed off.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Urum.text: Mongolian öröm: the thick skin of cream that forms on top of boiled milk, usually cow or yak milk. The milk is heated slowly and ladled to aerate it, so the fat rises to form a skin. The pot is left in a cool place for 12–24 hours, then the skin is lifted off in a folded sheet.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Lemon posset.text: A cold dessert of cream heated with sugar and set with lemon juice, dating from the late 19th century: a revival of the name of the old posset, a hot drink of milk curdled with wine or ale.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Syllabub.text: Syllabub refers to both a pudding and a beverage, both made by curdling cream or milk with an acid such as wine or cider. Both dishes were popular in British cuisine from the 16th to the 19th centuries. The holiday punch, sweet and frothy, was often considered a ladies' drink.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Gelato.text: Gelato refers to a specific type of ice cream of Italian origin. In Italian, gelato is the common word for all types of ice cream. Artisanal gelato in Italy generally contains 6–9% butterfat, which is lower than other styles of frozen dessert. Gelato typically contains 20–35% air, and more flavoring than other types of frozen desserts, giving it an intense flavor with creamy, smooth texture, density and richness that distinguishes it from other ice creams.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Soft serve.text: Soft serve, also known as soft ice cream, is a frozen dessert and variety of ice cream, similar to conventional ice cream, but softer and less dense due to more air being introduced during freezing. Soft serve has been sold commercially since the late 1930s in the United States.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Frozen custard.text: Frozen custard is a frozen dessert that is a type of ice cream made with egg yolks in addition to cream and sweetener, and an additional flavoring such as cocoa, vanilla, or fruit such as strawberries or peaches. It is usually kept at a warmer temperature compared to ice cream, and typically has a denser and thicker consistency.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Dondurma.text: Dondurma is the Turkish word for ice cream. Maraş dondurması or dövme dondurma is a Turkish variety associated with the city and province of Kahramanmaraş, known for its elastic texture and distinctive preparation. Traditional Maraş dondurması is made using goat's milk, salep, and sugar.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Makhan.text: The butter of the Indian subcontinent churned from dahi, set yoghurt made from whole milk or malai, rather than from fresh cream, traditionally by hand in an earthen pot. Eaten fresh, or heated slowly into desi ghee.

links.name: Journal of Food Science and Technology (2020)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Kibe.text: Ethiopian butter churned from ergo, naturally soured whole milk, in a clay pot or bottle gourd, then washed in cold water. Spiced and clarified, it becomes niter kibbeh.

links.name: Livestock Research for Rural Development 19(7) (2007), Yilma et al.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Zebda.text: The raw fresh butter of Morocco (zebda beldiya), churned from rayeb, raw milk left to sour for one to three days in an earthen jar or goatskin bag; the liquid left behind is lben. Salted and fermented, it becomes smen.

links.name: Benkirane et al., J. Microbiology, Biotechnology and Food Sciences (2022)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Lben.text: The Moroccan and Algerian fermented buttermilk. Raw milk is left to sour on its own at room temperature until it sets, then churned to separate raw butter (zebda beldia). The tangy skimmed liquid that remains is lben. It keeps only a few days.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Chaas.text: Chaas is a curd-based drink popular across the Indian subcontinent.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Rob.text: The sour buttermilk of Sudan: milk is left to sour for about a day, then shaken in a gourd until the butter (fursa) separates, and the liquid left over is drunk as it is.

links.name: FAO, The technology of traditional milk products in developing countries

sources.text: Written from this source.

Arera.text: The buttermilk left in Ethiopia after kibe is churned from ergo, soured milk: drunk as it is, or heated to make ayib cheese.

links.name: Food Science & Nutrition (2024), review of Ethiopian fermented milk products

sources.text: Written from this source.

Prostokvasha.text: The Russian soured milk. Traditionally milk was left to sour on its own or started with some ready soured milk. Factory versions use pure cultures that define the type: mesophilic lactococci for ordinary prostokvasha, thermophilic streptococci with Lactobacillus bulgaricus for the Mechnikov kind.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Clabber.text: Clabber is a type of soured milk. It is produced by allowing unpasteurized milk to turn sour (ferment) at a specific humidity and temperature. Over time, the milk thickens or curdles into a yogurt-like consistency with a strong, sour flavor. According to Joy of Cooking, "Clabber... is milk that has soured to the stage of a firm curd but not to a separation of the whey."

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Långfil.text: A Swedish fermented milk with a cohesive, stretchy ('long') texture and mild sourness. It is cultured slowly at low temperature with Lactococcus lactis subsp. cremoris strains that make exopolysaccharides. It was traditional in northern and central Sweden and western Finland, where a dried cloth soaked in old fil carried the culture.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Viili.text: Viili (Finnish) or Fil (Swedish) is a mesophilic fermented milk product found in the Nordic countries, particularly Finland and Sweden. Viili is similar to yoghurt or kefir, but when left unmixed, its texture is malleable, or "long". The metabolism of the bacteria used in the fermentation also gives viili a slightly different taste.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Tätmjölk.text: A ropy soured milk of central and northern Sweden, traditionally made long and stringy with butterwort (Pinguicula, in Swedish tätört) or with a starter kept from an earlier batch. On summer farms (fäbodar) it kept for months.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Varenets.text: Varenets, sometimes anglicised as stewler or simmeler, is a fermented milk product that is popular in Russia. Similar to ryazhenka, it is made by adding sour cream (smetana) to baked milk.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Bioghurt.text: A mild yoghurt culture and product name from Germany, introduced in 1956: Streptococcus thermophilus with Lactobacillus acidophilus in place of the sharper Lactobacillus bulgaricus, so the yoghurt sours less. Its sister culture Biogarde adds bifidobacteria.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Actimel.text: Actimel is a probiotic yoghurt-type drink produced by the French company Danone.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Activia.text: Activia is a brand of yoghurt made by the French company Danone, fermented with the two yoghurt bacteria and its own strain of Bifidobacterium animalis.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Yakult.text: Yakult is a Japanese sweetened probiotic milk beverage fermented with the bacteria strain Lacticaseibacillus casei Shirota. It is sold by Yakult Honsha, based in Tokyo. The name "Yakult" was coined from jahurto, an Esperanto word meaning "yogurt".

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Acidophilus milk.text: Milk fermented with Lactobacillus acidophilus. Interest in it goes back about 80 years, to when it was used to treat intestinal infections. Later studies looked at lactose digestion, cholesterol and cancer, and concluded that any benefit depends on careful choice of strain.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Tarag.text: Mongolian soured milk, made from cow's, yak's, goat's or sheep's milk. Eaten as it is, dried into aaruul, or, made from cow's or yak's milk, distilled into shimiin arkhi.

links.name: Bianquis, Les alcools de lait en Mongolie (OCHA, 2004)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Matsoni.text: Matzoon or matsoni is a fermented milk product of Armenian origin found in Armenia and Georgia. The Caspian Sea yogurt commercialized in Japan is said to be the same type of yogurt as matzoon, but a comparison of microbiota and viscosity found that the two are entirely different. Georgian matsoni has been a protected geographical indication in Georgia since 24 January 2012.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Labneh.text: The Levantine strained yogurt, taken further than Greek yogurt. In Lebanon and other Middle Eastern countries, set yogurt is drained in cloth bags until it reaches about 23–25% solids and 9–11% fat. Commercial labneh keeps for two to three weeks in the fridge.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Chakka.text: Indian yoghurt strained in muslin until it is thick and semi-solid. Sweetened and spiced with cardamom and saffron, it becomes shrikhand.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Suzma.text: Strained yoghurt of Central Asia, drained from qatiq until it is thick; in Turkey it is süzme yoğurt, or kese yoğurdu, 'bag yoghurt'. Dried further, it becomes qurut.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Doogh.text: Doogh is a cold and savoury Persian drink. It is made with fermented milk. Unlike ayran, a yoghurt drink of Turkish origin, doogh is not diluted yogurt. According to the Iranian Ministry of Food Standards, doogh "is a drink resulting from lactic fermentation of milk whose dry matter is standardized by diluting yogurt or buttermilk ."

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Tan.text: The Armenian yogurt drink: matsun (Armenian yogurt) thinned with water and salted, sometimes with herbs. It is drunk across the Caucasus mountains, and industrial versions have been sold since the 1990s.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Mastaw.text: The Kurdish yogurt drink, also called ava mast: yogurt and salt mixed with water. Yogurt (mast) is the most widely eaten fermented dairy product among Kurds.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Salted lassi.text: Lassi is a yogurt–based beverage with a smoothie-like consistency. The word 'lassi' for the drink is a borrowing from Hindi, first attested in 1882; its ultimate origin is unclear, and has been suggested as derived ultimately from Sanskrit lasya (stickiness) or rasah (juice).

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Kashk.text: Iran's kashk: yoghurt churned with water to take off the butter, the defatted liquid boiled, drained in linen bags, salted, shaped and sun-dried into hard, protein-rich balls, which are later ground and soaked back into liquid kashk.

links.name: Say, Soltani & Güzeler, Pamukkale Univ. J. Eng. Sci. (2015)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Qurut.text: The dried fermented-milk cheese of the Kazakhs and other Central Asian nomads; the name comes from the Turkic word for ‘dry’. Milk is soured with yoghurt from an earlier batch, boiled, and the curd pressed in cloth, salted, rolled into small balls and sun-dried for up to two weeks. It keeps for over a year.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Chortan.text: The Armenian name (չորթան) for dried tan, the buttermilk left after butter is churned from matsun; dried into a hard, keeping food like the qurut of Central Asia.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Aaruul.text: Mongolian dried curd, a long-standing portable food of herding families. Most is made from the yoghurt of cows or yaks, although any livestock milk or yoghurt can be used. The curd is spread on the sloping roof of the ger to dry in the sun, then shaped. Sugar is sometimes added. Once hard, it keeps for a long time.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Choormog.text: The Mongolian name (khoormog) for fermented camel's milk, left to sour naturally and made by camel-herding households, mostly in the Gobi, as airag is from mare's milk.

links.name: FAO, One Country One Priority Product: Mongolia

sources.text: Written from this source.

Chal.text: Chal is the Turkmen fermented camel milk, a sparkling white, sour drink. It is the regional counterpart of Kazakh shubat, and is difficult to export because it is perishable.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Shubat.text: Chal, also shubat or khoormog, is a Turkic and Mongolic beverage of fermented camel milk, sparkling white with a sour flavor, popular in Central Asia — particularly in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. In Kazakhstan the drink is known as shubat, and is a staple summer food. Due to preparation requirements and perishable nature, chal has proved difficult to export. Agaran is collected from the surface of chal.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Gariss.text: Fermented camel milk made by camel herders in the pastoral areas of Sudan. Traditionally it ferments while the herd is on the move: the jolting of the camel's walk shakes the milk in its bag. Herders start each batch with soured product kept back from earlier batches instead of a pure culture.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Suusac.text: Fermented camel milk from the pastoralist herds of northern Kenya, also spelled suusa. Raw camel milk is left to sour by itself, with no starter culture. Its containers are first fumigated with smoke from particular woods, which helps it keep and gives it a smoky taste. Women do the processing.

links.name: African Journal of Food, Agriculture, Nutrition and Development (2013)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Dhanaan.text: Fermented camel's milk of the Somali herders of eastern Ethiopia, left to sour on its own in a clean or smoked container; the smoke, from woods such as wild olive, helps it keep.

links.name: Seifu, Livestock Research for Rural Development (2007)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Shimiin arkhi.text: Mongolian milk spirit, distilled from fermented cow's or yak's milk (tarag) in a still of a cauldron, a wooden barrel and a second pot of cold water, to about 10–16 % alcohol. Rarer than airag, it is opened with an offering to the spirits.

links.name: Bianquis, Les alcools de lait en Mongolie (OCHA, 2004)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Araka.text: The milk spirit of the Khakas of southern Siberia, distilled from airan, soured milk, and formerly also from kumis.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Tarasun.text: The Buryat milk spirit, distilled from soured mare's or cow's milk; poured as an offering at festivals and shamanic rites as well as drunk.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Araga.text: The Tuvan milk spirit, distilled from khoitpak, a soured milk drink, and also from kumis; made only in summer, when there was milk to spare.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Artz.text: Arkhi distilled a second time, stronger than the first, at around 30 % alcohol: in Mongolian, arz.

links.name: Bianquis, Les alcools de lait en Mongolie (OCHA, 2004)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Khorz.text: Arz distilled once more (a third distillation), stronger still.

links.name: Mongolian Academy of Sciences dictionary (mongoltoli.mn), entry арз

sources.text: Written from this source.

Harzer.text: A German sour-milk cheese from the northern Harz foothills, though most is now made elsewhere. Crumbly, low-fat sour-milk quark from cow’s milk is shaped and coated with red-smear bacteria, ripening within days into a pungent cheese with under 10% fat in dry matter, often seasoned with caraway.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Olmützer Quargel.text: Olomoucké tvarůžky, also known as olomoucké syrečky or tvargle, English: Olomouc cheese, Olomouc curd cheese) is a ripened soft cheese made in Loštice, Olomouc Region, Czech Republic. The cheese is very easy to recognize by its strong scent, distinctive pungent taste and yellowish colour. It is named after the city of Olomouc where it was originally sold.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Tiroler Graukäse.text: Tyrolean grey cheese is a strongly flavoured, rennet-free cows-milk acid-curd quark made in the Tyrolean Alp valleys, Austria. It owes its name to the grey mold that usually grows on its rind. It is extremely low in fat and has a powerful penetrating smell. The cheese produced in Austria is registered as protected designation of origin (PDO), Austria generally indicated in German as g.U. under the official name Tiroler Graukäse. The registration of the PDO states that its production has been a significant element of Tyrolean peasant gastronomy for centuries. Graukäse produced in Italy is protected by a prodotti agroalimentari tradizionali (PAT) designation. Graukäse making became widespread on farms due to the simplicity of making and the availability of low-fat milk after the fat had been taken for use in butter making.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Handkäse.text: Handkäse is a German regional sour milk cheese and is a culinary specialty of Frankfurt am Main, Offenbach am Main, Darmstadt, Langen, and other parts of southern Hesse. It gets its name from the traditional way of producing it: forming it with one's own hands.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Mainzer.text: A German sour milk cheese named after Mainz and grouped with Harzer in the German cheese regulations: small low-fat cheeses of 25–125 g, made from sour milk quark and ripened with a yellow or red smear.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Rubing.text: Rubing is a firm, acid-set, non-melting, fresh goat milk farmer cheese made in the Yunnan Province of China by people of the Bai and Sani minorities. Its Bai name is youdbap, meaning "goat's milk".

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Rasgulla.text: Rasgulla is a syrupy dessert popular in the eastern part of India & South Asia. It is made from ball-shaped dumplings of chhena dough cooked in light sugar syrup until the syrup permeates the dumplings.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Sandesh.text: Sandesh is a Bengali dessert, originating from the undivided Bengal region in the eastern part of the Indian subcontinent, created with milk and sugar. Some recipes of sandesh call for the use of chhena or paneer instead of milk itself. Some people in the region of Dhaka make a variety of sandesh called pranahara which is softer and made with mawa and yogurt. Basirhat is known for its kachagolla sandesh. Historically, it can be seen that the culture of making this kachagolla in Basirhat is about 400 years old. The Gupo or Gufo style of sandesh from Guptipara is considered by some to be the "first branded sweet of Bengal".

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Rasmalai.text: Ras malai, also known as rasamalei or roshmalai, is a dessert that originated in the Bengal region of the Indian subcontinent. The dessert is called roshmalai in Bengali, ras malai in Hindi, and rasa malei in Odia. It is popular in India, Bangladesh, and Pakistan.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Wagashi.text: A soft cheese from northern Benin, made by women and mostly by the Peulh (Fulani). Fresh whole cow's milk is heated and curdled with an extract of the Sodom apple plant (Calotropis procera), whose enzyme does the work of rennet. The curd drains in small colanders. Some cheeses are dyed red with sorghum.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Dangke.text: Dangke is a type of cottage cheese produced in Enrekang, South Sulawesi, Indonesia, especially in Enrekang, Baraka, Anggeraja, and Alla districts. Dangke is processed by boiling fresh cattle or buffalo milk with sliced papaya leaves, stems, or unripe papaya fruits. Dangke is typically soaked in a brine solution overnight before being wrapped with banana leaves for masking the bitter taste caused by the addition of papaya leaves.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ginger milk curd.text: Ginger milk curd, also known as ginger-juice milk curd, ginger milk pudding or simply ginger milk, is a Chinese dessert originating from Shawan Ancient Town, Panyu District, Guangzhou in the Guangdong Province of southern China. The main ingredients are ginger, milk, and sugar. Water buffalo milk is traditionally used.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Queso fresco.text: Mexico's most popular fresh cheese, also widely eaten in the United States. Skimmed or partly skimmed milk is set with rennet at about 38 °C, and the curd is finely milled before salting, which makes the cheese crumbly. It is pressed only by its own weight, is not ripened and has a short shelf life.

links.name: Temas Selectos de Ingeniería de Alimentos (2012)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Panela.text: Queso panela is a fresh cheese common in Mexico made from pasteurized cow's milk. It is also known as queso canasta or queso de la canasta. It is derived from the Greek word for basket cheese. The cheese also has similarities to the Indian cheese paneer.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Robiola.text: Robiola is an Italian soft-ripened cheese of the stracchino family. It is from the Langhe region and made with varying proportions of cow's, goat's, and sheep's milk. One theory is that the cheese gets its name from the comune (municipality) of Robbio, in the province of Pavia; another that the name comes from the word rubeole (ruddy) because of the color of the seasoned rind.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Tomino.text: A small cheese from Piedmont, made from cow's or goat's milk or a mix of both. The milk is warmed with rennet and the curd is broken up finely and drained. Eaten fresh, it is soft, moist and white. Matured ones get a thin rind and a stronger smell and are often warmed in a pan or on soapstone.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Bel Paese.text: An industrial Italian cheese created by Egidio Galbani in 1906 and named after Antonio Stoppani’s book Il Bel Paese, whose author’s portrait appears on the wrapper. It is made from pasteurised cow’s milk and ripened for six to eight weeks, giving a mild, creamy cheese with 45–50% fat in dry matter.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Butterkäse.text: Butterkäse is a semi-soft, cow's milk cheese moderately popular in Germanic Europe, and occasionally seen in the rest of the cheese-eating world. Although primarily produced in Germany, some Butterkäse is produced in Wisconsin.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Saint-Paulin.text: Saint Paulin is a creamy, mild, semi-soft French cheese made from pasteurized cow's milk, originally made by Trappist monks at Saint Paulin. It is a buttery cheese, but firm enough for slicing. Saint Paulin is similar to Havarti and Esrom, and is suited to serving as a table or dessert cheese; it is often served with fruit and light wine. Genuine Saint Paulin has an edible yellow-orange rind. It is ripened in a round loaf with slightly protruding sides, and matures in about four weeks.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Stracchino.text: Stracchino, also known as crescenza, is an Italian cow's milk cheese typical of the regions of Lombardy, Tuscany, Veneto, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, and Liguria. It is eaten very young, has no rind and has a very soft, creamy texture and normally a mild, slightly acidic flavour. It is normally square in shape.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Cuartirolo.text: An Argentine soft cheese defined in the national food code: whole or standardised milk is soured with lactic cultures and set with rennet, and the curd is moulded, pressed, salted and ripened for at least 20 days. The result is a high-moisture, fatty cheese with a soft, slightly acidic, white-to-yellowish paste.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Manchego.text: Manchego is a cheese made in the La Mancha region of Spain from the milk of sheep of the Manchega breed. It is aged between 60 days and 2 years.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Tilsiter.text: Tilsit cheese or Tilsiter cheese is a pale yellow semihard smear-ripened cheese, created in the mid-19th century by Prussian-Swiss settlers, the Westphal family, from the Emmental valley. The original buildings from the cheese plant still exist in Sovetsk, Russia, formerly Tilsit, on the Neman River, in the former German province of East Prussia.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Havarti.text: Havarti or cream Havarti is a semisoft Danish cow's milk cheese. It can be sliced, grilled, or melted.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Monterey Jack.text: Monterey Jack, sometimes shortened to Jack, is a Californian white, semi-hard cheese made using cow's milk, with a mild flavor and slight sweetness. Originating in Monterey, on the Central Coast of California, the cheese has been called "a vestige of Spanish rule in the early nineteenth century, deriving from a Franciscan monastic style of farmer's cheese".

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Morbier.text: Morbier is a semi-soft cows' milk cheese of France named after the small village of Morbier in Franche-Comté. It is ivory colored, soft and slightly elastic, and is immediately recognizable by the distinctive thin black layer separating it horizontally in the middle. It has a yellowish, sticky rind.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Parmigiano Reggiano.text: Parmesan is an Italian hard, granular cheese produced from cow's milk and aged at least 12 months. It is a grana-type cheese, along with Grana Padano, the historic Granone Lodigiano, and others.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Grana Padano.text: Grana Padano is an Italian cheese originating in the Po Valley. It is similar to Parmesan but with less strict regulations governing its production. This hard, crumbly-textured cheese is made with unpasteurized cows' milk that is semi-skimmed. To preserve the authenticity of the manufacturing processes and raw materials used to make this cheese, Grana Padano was registered as a denominazione di origine controllata (DOC) in 1955, and as a European Union protected designation of origin (PDO) in 1996. Outside of the EU, its name is protected in several other countries on the basis of the Lisbon Agreement and bilateral agreements.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Pecorino Romano.text: Pecorino romano is a hard, salty Italian cheese made from sheep milk, often used for grating over pasta or other dishes. The name pecorino means 'ovine' or 'of sheep' in Italian; the name of the cheese, although protected, is a description rather than a brand: [formaggio] pecorino romano means 'sheep's [cheese] of Rome'.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Sbrinz.text: Sbrinz is a very hard cheese produced in Central Switzerland. It is often used as grated cheese in Swiss cuisine, although it is also eaten in small pieces. The cheese is produced in only 42 dairies in Central Switzerland. Only local cow's milk is used when producing this cheese. It is kept in the region until ready for consumption. It is the hardest of Swiss cheeses together with Berner Hobelkäse.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Mahón.text: Mahón cheese is a soft to hard white cheese made from cows' milk, named after the town and natural port of Mahón, on the island of Menorca off the Mediterranean coast of Spain. Menorca is known for its cheese production.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Brie de Meaux.text: Brie de Meaux is a French brie cheese of the Brie region and a designated AOC product since 1980. Its name comes from the town of Meaux in the Brie region. As of 2003, 6,774 tonnes were produced annually.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Camembert de Normandie.text: Camembert is a moist, soft, creamy, surface-ripened cow's milk cheese. It was first made in the late 18th century in Camembert, Normandy, in northwest France. It is sometimes compared in look, taste and texture to brie cheese, albeit with a slightly lower butterfat content than brie's typical 20–25% by weight.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Coulommiers.text: Coulommiers is a soft ripened cheese from Coulommiers, Seine-et-Marne, France. It is made from cow's milk, and is usually in the shape of a disc with white, bloomy, edible Penicillium candidum rind. When produced as an artisanal or "farmhouse" cheese from unpasteurized milk, it has some reddish blush in parts of the rind. The period of ripening when made of pasteurised whole milk is about four to six weeks. The fat content is 40 per cent.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Chaource.text: Chaource is a French cheese, originally manufactured in the village of Chaource in the Champagne-Ardenne region.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Brillat-Savarin.text: Brillat-Savarin is a soft-ripened triple cream cow's milk cheese with at least 72% fat in dry matter. It has a natural, bloomy rind. It was created in 1890 as "Excelsior" or "Délice des gourmets" by the Dubuc family, near Forges-les-Eaux in Seine-Maritime. Brillat-Savarin is produced all year round, mainly in Normandy, and also in Burgundy.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Roquefort.text: Roquefort is a sheep-milk blue cheese from southern France. EU law dictates that only those cheeses aged in the natural Combalou caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon may bear the name "Roquefort", as it is a recognised geographical indication and has a protected designation of origin.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Gorgonzola.text: Gorgonzola is an Italian blue cheese made from unskimmed cow's milk, believed to have been created in the 9th century. Today the use of its name is controlled under the criteria of a protected designation of origin (PDO).

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Stilton.text: Stilton is an English cheese, produced in two varieties: blue, which has Penicillium roqueforti added to generate a characteristic smell and taste, and white, which does not. Both have been granted the status of a protected designation of origin (PDO) by the European Commission, requiring that only such cheese produced in the three counties of Derbyshire, Leicestershire and Nottinghamshire may be called Stilton. The cheese takes its name from the village of Stilton, now in Cambridgeshire, where the cheese was originally sold. Today, cheese made there cannot be named Stilton because of the PDO.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Danish Blue.text: Danablu, often marketed under the trademark Danish Blue Cheese within North America, is a strong, blue-veined cheese. This semi-soft creamy cheese is typically drum- or block-shaped and has a yellowish, slightly moist, edible rind. Made from full fat cow's milk and homogenized cream, it has a fat content of 25–30% and is aged for eight to twelve weeks.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Cabrales.text: Cabrales is a blue cheese made in the artisan tradition by rural dairy farmers in Asturias, Spain. This cheese can be made from pure, unpasteurized cow’s milk or blended in the traditional manner with goat and/or sheep milk, which lends the cheese a stronger, spicier flavor.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Époisses.text: Époisses, also known as Époisses de Bourgogne, is a legally demarcated cheese made in the village of Époisses and its environs, in the département of Côte-d'Or, about halfway between Dijon and Auxerre, in the former duchy of Burgundy, France, from agricultural processes and resources traditionally found in that region.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Munster.text: Munster, Munster-géromé, or (Alsatian) Minschterkaas, is a soft cheese with a strong taste and aroma, made mainly from milk first produced in the Vosges, between the Alsace, Lorraine and Franche-Comté regions in France. The name "Munster" is derived from the Alsatian town of Munster, where, among Vosgian abbeys and monasteries, the cheese was conserved and matured in monks' cellars. "Géromé", a variant from munster, comes from the Vosgien patois pronunciation of the town of Gérardmer, located on the Lorrain side of the Vosges mountains, where it originates.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Limburger.text: Limburger, commonly known as Limburg, is a cheese that originated in the Herve area of the historical Duchy of Limburg, which had its capital in Limbourg-sur-Vesdre, now in the French-speaking Belgian province of Liège. The cheese is especially known for its strong smell caused by the bacterium Brevibacterium linens.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Taleggio.text: Taleggio is a semisoft washed-rind Italian cheese named after Val Taleggio, Italy. The cheese has a thin, edible rind and a strong aroma, but its flavour is comparatively mild with an unusual fruity tang. The rind is a pinkish-brown, and the interior is creamy and pale yellow. It has a protected designation of origin so that only such cheese produced in the Lombardy or Piedmont regions of Italy may be designated as Taleggio.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Herve.text: A soft, washed-rind cow's-milk cheese from the Pays de Herve in Belgium's Liège province, with PDO status since 1996. It is salted in brine or with coarse salt and ripened for four to eight weeks. Brevibacterium linens gives the rind its reddish colour and the cheese its strong flavour. Raw or pasteurised milk may be used.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Emmentaler.text: Emmental is a yellow, medium-hard cheese with natural holes that originated in the Emme Valley in Switzerland. It is classified as a Swiss-type cheese.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Gruyère.text: Gruyère is a hard Swiss cheese that originated in the Fribourg, Vaud, Neuchâtel, Jura, and Bern cantons in Switzerland. It is named after the town of Gruyères in Fribourg. In 2001, Gruyère gained the appellation d'origine contrôlée (AOC), which became the appellation d'origine protégée (AOP) as of 2013.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Comté.text: Comté, also known as Gruyère de Comté, is a hard cheese made from unpasteurised cow's milk in eastern France. The production of Comté is the largest of the Protected designation of origin (PDO) cheeses made in France.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Beaufort.text: Beaufort is a firm, raw cow's milk cheese associated with the gruyère family. An Alpine cheese, it is produced in Beaufortain, Tarentaise valley and Maurienne, which are located in the Savoie region of the French Alps.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Appenzeller.text: Appenzeller cheese is a hard cow's-milk washed-rind cheese produced in the Appenzellerland region of northeast Switzerland, in the two modern-day cantons of Appenzell Innerrhoden and Appenzell Ausserrhoden. It is classified as a Swiss-type or Alpine cheese.

Cheddar.text: Cheddar cheese is a natural cheese that is relatively hard, off-white, and sometimes sharp-tasting. It originates from the village of Cheddar in Somerset, South West England.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Red Leicester.text: Red Leicester is an English cheese similar to Cheddar cheese, but crumbly in texture. It is typically aged 6 to 12 months. The rind is reddish-orange with a powdery mould on it. Since the 18th century, it has been coloured orange by the addition of annatto extract during manufacture. It is a cow's milk cheese, and is named after the city of Leicester, or the ceremonial county it is located in, Leicestershire.

Double Gloucester.text: Gloucester is a traditional, semi-hard cheese which has been made in Gloucestershire, England, since the 16th century. There are two varieties of the cheese, Single and Double; both are traditionally made from milk from Gloucester cattle. Both types have a natural rind and a hard texture, but Single Gloucester is more crumbly, lighter in texture and lower in fat. Double Gloucester is allowed to age for longer periods than Single, and it has a stronger and more savoury flavour. It is also slightly firmer. The wild flower Galium verum, known colloquially as lady's bedstraw, was originally responsible for the distinctively yellow colour of Double Gloucester cheese.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Dunlop.text: Dunlop is a mild cheese or 'sweet-milk cheese' from Dunlop, East Ayrshire, Scotland. It resembles a soft Cheddar cheese in texture. Though it fell out of popularity some time after the end of the Second World War, it is now appreciated for its value in various recipes and for eating on its own or with a dram of whisky.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Cheese curds.text: Cheese curds are moist pieces of curdled milk, eaten either alone as a snack, or used in prepared dishes. They are consumed throughout the United States and Canada. In addition to being eaten alone, they are popular in Quebec, as part of the dish poutine, and in Wisconsin and Minnesota where they can be served breaded and deep fried. Curds are sometimes referred to as "squeaky cheese" or fromage en grain.

Gouda.text: Gouda cheese is a family of yellow cow's milk cheeses originally from the Netherlands. Gouda ranges from young and elastic to old and hard, and from low-fat to high-fat.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Edam.text: Edam is a semi-hard cheese that originated in the Netherlands, and is named after the town of Edam in the province of North Holland. Edam is traditionally sold in flat-ended spheres with a pale yellow interior and a coat, or rind, of red paraffin wax. Edam ages and travels well and hardens, instead of spoiling, for an extended period. These qualities made it the world's most popular cheese between the 14th and 18th centuries, both at sea and in remote colonies.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Colby.text: Colby is a semihard orange cheese made from cow's milk. It is named after the U.S. city of Colby, Wisconsin, where it was first developed in 1885 and quickly became popular. Today the cheese is typically used in snacks, sandwiches, and salads.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Leyden.text: Leyden, from Dutch: Leidse kaas, is a semi-hard, cumin and caraway seed flavoured cheese made in the Netherlands from cow's milk. It is made both in factories and on farms, historically in the Leiden area.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Maasdam.text: Maasdam cheese is an Emmental-style Dutch cheese. Made from cow's milk, it is aged for at least four weeks. It ripens faster than other cheeses made in the Netherlands. Maasdam has internal voids, or holes from the ripening process, and a smooth, yellow rind. Sometimes, it is waxed like Gouda. The cheese was created to compete with Swiss Emmentaler cheeses by being less expensive and quicker to produce. In the process of making a cheese with the same general components as Swiss cheeses, the Dutch ended up with a cheese that is nutty and sweet, but softer than Emmental, due to a higher moisture content.

Casu marzu.text: Casu martzu is a Sardinian sheep milk cheese that contains live fly maggots.

Casgiu merzu.text: The Corsican counterpart of Sardinian casu martzu, made especially in villages of southern Corsica: a cheese left open to cheese flies (Piophila casei), whose larvae break it down until it is very soft and pungent.

Marcetto.text: A spreadable cheese from the mountains of Abruzzo, made chiefly around Castel del Monte, also called cacio or pecorino marcetto. Cheese flies (Piophila casei) lay eggs in cracks in a ripening raw-milk pecorino. Their larvae break down the proteins and turn the paste into a very sharp cream, which is packed into glass or terracotta jars.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Mimolette.text: Mimolette is a cheese traditionally produced around the city of Lille, France. In France it is also known as boule de Lille after its city of origin, or vieux Hollande because it was originally inspired by the Dutch Edam cheese.

Milbenkäse.text: Milbenkäse, called Mellnkase in the local dialect and often known as Spinnenkäse, is a German speciality cheese. It is made by flavouring balls of quark with caraway and salt, allowing them to dry, and then leaving them in a wooden box containing rye flour and cheese mites for about three months. An enzyme in the digestive juices excreted by the mites causes the cheese to ripen. Milbenkäse tastes similar to Harzer cheese, but with a bitter note and a zesty aftertaste. Mites clinging to the cheese rind are consumed along with the cheese.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

American cheese.text: American cheese is a type of processed cheese made from cheddar, Colby, or similar cheeses, in conjunction with sodium citrate, which permits the cheese to be pasteurized without its components separating. It is mild with a creamy texture and salty flavor, has a medium-firm consistency, and has a low melting point. It is typically yellow or white in color; yellow American cheese is seasoned and colored with annatto.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Cancoillotte.text: Cancoillotte or cancoyotte is a runny French cheese made from metton cheese, and produced principally in Franche-Comté, but also Lorraine and Luxembourg, where it is also called Kachkéis or Kochkäse in German. It is a typical cheese in Franc-Comtois gastronomy. It is eaten all year around, served cold or hot.

Requeijão (Portugal).text: Requeijão is a whey cheese produced in Portugal and Brazil. It is similar to ricotta and is used to make cheese spreads and as an ingredient in some pastries, such as queijada.

Requeijão cremoso.text: The Brazilian spreadable cheese sold in cups, made by melting a drained, washed milk curd with cream or butter and melting salts. Not the Portuguese whey cheese of the same name, which is closer to ricotta.

Plavleny syrok.text: The small foil-wrapped processed cheese of the Soviet Union and Russia. The best known, Druzhba, was developed in 1960 at Moscow's Karat plant and is still made to the same recipe.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Velveeta.text: Velveeta is a brand name for a processed cheese similar to American cheese. It was developed in 1918 by Emil Frey (1867–1951) of the Monroe Cheese Company in Monroe, New York. In 1923, The Velveeta Cheese Company was incorporated as a separate company. In 1925, it advertised two varieties, Swiss and American. The firm was purchased by Kraft Foods Inc. in 1927.

Halloumi.text: Halloumi, or haloumi, is a type of dairy product made with milk originating from Cyprus. It is traditionally made from a mixture of goat milk and sheep's milk; however, due to lower cost of cow's milk and price sensitivity of consumers, modern halloumi increasingly contains cow's milk.

Leipäjuusto.text: Bread cheese, sometimes known in the United States as Finnish squeaky cheese, is a Finnish fresh cheese traditionally made from cow's colostrum. In the US, cow's milk is generally used but can also be made with goat milk. Commercially available versions are typically made from cow's milk. The cheese originally comes from Southern Ostrobothnia, Northern Finland, and Kainuu.

Burrata.text: Burrata is an Italian fresh cheese from Apulia: a shell of pasta filata mozzarella filled with stracciatella and cream.

Stracciatella di bufala.text: Stracciatella made from buffalo milk: shredded stretched curd mixed with cream.

Bryndza podhalańska.text: Bryndza Podhalańska is a Polish PDO cheese from the Podhale region, made from sheep milk with at most 40% cow milk.

Slovenská bryndza.text: Slovenská bryndza is a Slovak PGI cheese: ground sheep lump cheese, or sheep lump cheese mixed with up to 50% cow lump cheese, with salt (OJ C 232/2007).

Queso para freír.text: A firm, salty white cheese from the Spanish-speaking Caribbean and Central America, made to be sliced and fried rather than melted. In the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua it is the cheese used for queso frito, slices of fried cheese.

Mozzarella di bufala.text: Buffalo mozzarella is a mozzarella made from the milk of the Italian Mediterranean buffalo. A fresh, soft pasta filata cheese, it is traditionally produced in Campania, particularly in the provinces of Caserta and Salerno.

Provolone.text: Provolone is an Italian semi-hard cheese made from cow's milk. It is an aged pasta filata ('stretched-curd') cheese originating in the Campania region, near Vesuvius, where it is still produced in pear, sausage, or cone shapes 10 to 15 cm long. Provolone-type cheeses are also produced in other countries. The most important provolone production region today is northwestern Italy and, in particular, the city of Cremona. Provolone, provola, and provoleta are versions of the same basic cheese. Some versions of provolone are smoked.

Provoleta.text: Provoleta is an Argentine variant of provolone cheese described as "Argentine pulled-curd provolone cheese". It can be heated on a grill, or indoors in a cast-iron pan. The cheese is firm and can hold its shape when grilled.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Caciocavallo.text: Caciocavallo is a type of pasta filata ('stretched-curd') cheese made out of sheep's or cow's milk. It is produced throughout southern Italy, particularly in the Apennine Mountains and in the Gargano peninsula. Shaped like a teardrop, it is similar in taste to the aged southern Italian provolone cheese, with a hard edible rind.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Kashkaval.text: Kashkaval is a type of cheese made from the milk of cows, sheep, goats, or a mixture thereof, popular in the Balkans, Turkey, and the Levant. In Hungary, kashkaval refers specifically to this type of cheese, whereas, in the rest of the Balkans, Turkey and the Levant, the term is often used to refer to all yellow cheeses. In English-language menus in Bulgaria, kashkaval is translated as 'yellow cheese'.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Feta.text: Feta is a Greek white brined cheese made from sheep's milk or from a mixture of sheep and goat's milk. It is soft, with small or no holes, and no skin. Crumbly with a slightly grainy texture, it is formed into large blocks and aged in brine. Its flavour is tangy and salty, ranging from mild to sharp. Feta is used in salads, such as Greek salad, and in pastries, notably the filo-based Greek dishes spanakopita 'spinach pie', and tyropita 'cheese pie'. It is often served with olive oil or olives, and sprinkled with aromatic herbs such as oregano. It can also be served cooked, as part of a sandwich, in omelettes, and many other dishes.

Sirene.text: Sirene, also known as "white brine sirene", is a type of brined cheese originating from Bulgaria. It is made from the milk of goats, sheep, cows, buffalo or a mixture thereof. It is slightly crumbly, with at least 46–48% of dry matter containing 44–48% of fat. It is commonly produced in blocks, and has a slightly grainy texture. It is used as a table cheese, in salads, and in baking.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Domiati.text: Domiati cheese, also referred to as "white cheese", is a soft white salty cheese made primarily in Egypt, but also in Sudan and other Middle Eastern countries. Typically made from buffalo milk, cow milk, or a mixture, it can also be made from other milks, such as sheep, goat or camel milk. It is the most common Egyptian cheese. Unlike feta and other white cheeses, salt is added directly to the milk, before rennet is added. It is named after the seaport city of Damietta (دمياط).

Akkawi.text: Akkawi cheese is a white brine cheese from the Levant region, named after the Palestinian city of Acre.

Telemea.text: Telemea is the name of a Romanian cheese traditionally made of sheep's milk. Nowadays the term encompasses cheese made out of cow's milk, and in some cases of goat's, or buffalo's milk.

Soft chhurpi.text: A soft, fresh cheese of Nepal, Bhutan, Tibet and Sikkim, made by heating buttermilk until it curdles and hanging the curd in cloth to drain; cooked with greens, ground into chutney or added to soup.

Datshi.text: Bhutan's everyday cheese and the base of ema datshi, the chilli-and-cheese curry. Cow's milk is fermented and churned for butter. The leftover buttermilk is gently heated over a flame until the casein curdles. The curd is squeezed free of whey and rolled into small balls. A matured form is called zoety.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Ayib.text: A soft cottage-type cheese from the Ethiopian highlands. Fermented whole milk (ergo) is churned for butter, and the leftover buttermilk is heated until curd and whey separate. The curd is then drained through cloth. About six litres of buttermilk make one kilogram of ayib.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Çökelek.text: Çökelek is a fermented and acid/heat coagulated fresh cheese from Turkey and Azerbaijan. It can be produced from heating fermented buttermaking by-products such as buttermilk (yayıkaltı), though skimmed milk yogurt can also be used as a starting material. It can also be obtained from yayık ayranı through heat exposure. Despite its similar appearance, it is distinct from Lor, a form of curdled whey product similar to cottage cheese. Keş, şor, ekşimik and minci are different local names associated with çökelek.

Peda.text: Peda, pedha or pera is an Indian sweet that originated in the city of Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India. Traditionally prepared as thick, semi-soft round balls, its main ingredients are khoa, sugar and traditional flavourings including cardamom seeds. It is brown in colour. Variant spellings and names for the dessert include pedha, penda and pera and it is found in several varities in north India.

Barfi.text: Barfi or burfi is a milk-based sweet from the Indian subcontinent with a fudge-like consistency. It is consumed throughout India and Pakistan and is especially popular in North India. Barfi is often served at celebrations and religious festivals such as Diwali and Holi.

Kalakand.text: Kalakand is a sweet cheese confection from India. It has been described as "akin to Italian cheesecake, firmer in texture than milk cake, but softer than burfis."

Gulab jamun.text: Gulab jamun is a sweet dessert or mithai which had originated in the Indian subcontinent, and is popular in India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan and Burmese cuisines.

Cajeta.text: The Mexican goat's-milk version of dulce de leche, a thick, runny caramel. Goat's milk is simmered for several hours in a copper pan with sugar, bicarbonate of soda and a starch. It is stirred constantly until it thickens and turns light brown. It may be flavoured with vanilla, cinnamon or rum.

Arequipe.text: Colombia's and Venezuela's dulce de leche, simmered from milk and sugar until it is thick and caramel brown.

Requesón.text: A soft, cheap fresh cheese made from the curd recovered from the whey left over after cheesemaking. In Mexico it is popular, spoils quickly, and is used like fresh cheese in gorditas, quesadillas, empanadas and sweet breads, or eaten with honey or jam.

Brocciu.text: Brocciu is a Corsican cheese produced from a combination of milk and whey, giving it some of the characteristics of whey cheese. It is produced from ewe's milk. It is notable as a substitute for lactose-rich Italian ricotta, as brocciu contains less lactose.

Mizithra.text: Mizithra or myzithra is a Greek whey cheese or mixed milk-whey cheese from sheep or goats, or both. It is sold both as a fresh cheese, similar to Italian ricotta, and as a salt-dried grating cheese, similar to Italian ricotta salata. The ratio of milk to whey is usually 7 to 3.

Manouri.text: Manouri is a Greek semi-soft, fresh white mixed milk-whey cheese made from goat or sheep milk as a by-product following the production of feta. It is produced primarily in Thessalia and Macedonia in central and northern Greece.

Žinčica.text: Žinčica, Žinčice, Żętyca, Жентиця, or Zyntyca, Jintiță is a drink made of sheep milk whey similar to kefir consumed mostly in Slovakia and Poland. It is a by-product in the process of making bryndza cheese.

Sýra.text: Icelandic fermented whey. Whey drained from skyr or cheese is left to ferment until lactic acid bacteria turn its milk sugar sour. Mixed with water it made a common drink, sýrublanda. Before salt and refrigeration became common, food was stored in barrels of it; this sour-pickled food, súrmatur, is still eaten at the midwinter Þorri feasts.

Sodium caseinate.text: A milk-protein powder made from acid casein. Skimmed milk is acidified so its casein precipitates; the curd is washed, neutralised with sodium hydroxide or another sodium alkali, and dried. At least 90% protein, it is used in coffee whiteners, whipped toppings, nutritional products and bakery goods.

Calcium caseinate.text: Acid casein reacted with calcium hydroxide and dried: a protein powder that disperses in water to a white, milky liquid, used in drinks, nutrition bars, creamers and toppings.

Milk paint.text: A historic water-based paint, also called casein paint, made from milk, slaked (hydrated) lime and pigment. Oil was often added to make a stronger emulsion, and recipes called for many other additives to improve durability. It was used on interiors and also on exterior surfaces.

Casein tempera.text: Paint whose binder is casein dissolved in an alkali, usually lime, or ammonium carbonate or borax; it dries fast to a matt film that becomes water-resistant with time. Used for murals, and by commercial illustrators until the late 1960s.

Casein distemper.text: A 'washable' form of distemper, the chalk-based matt finish used on British plaster walls and ceilings from the mid-18th century. Ordinary distemper is bound with animal glue and rubs off easily. Adding casein, a by-product of cheesemaking, as a binder made the finish more durable.

Jameed.text: Jordan's hard, dry skimmed yogurt, made mainly from sheep's milk on a small scale. Traditionally the yogurt is churned to take off the butter, and the skimmed remainder is salted and dried. Market samples average about 85% solids and 16% salt, which lets it keep for months.

Meekiri.text: The traditional fermented buffalo-milk gel of Sri Lanka, set by back-slopping in a clay pot. It is thicker, creamier and whiter than cow's-milk yoghurt and is eaten with kithul palm treacle.

Nunu.text: A yoghurt-like spontaneously fermented milk of Ghana and West Africa, made from raw cow's milk.

Asiago.text: An Italian cow-milk cheese from the Veneto and Trentino plateau, made as fresh Pressato and as aged d'Allevo; DOP since 1996.

Montasio.text: A cow-milk cheese from Friuli-Venezia Giulia and the Veneto, aged at least two months and sometimes a year or more; PDO since 1986.

Kasseri.text: Kasseri is a Greek pasta filata cheese made from sheep's milk, with at most 20 % goat's milk. It is made in Thessaly, Macedonia, Lesbos and Xanthi, and holds a Greek PDO. Turkish kaşar and Balkan kashkaval are the same family.

Scamorza.text: Scamorza is an Italian stretched-curd cheese from southern Italy, made from cow's milk (in Bari also sheep's). It is hung tied by a string, which gives it a pear shape, and is also sold smoked (affumicata).

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Suluguni.text: Suluguni is a Georgian brined stretched-curd cheese from Samegrelo, made from cow's, buffalo's or mixed milk. It has a Georgian geographical indication from 2012.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Beyaz peynir.text: Beyaz peynir is the Turkish white cheese, traditionally made from unpasteurised sheep's milk (cow's or goat's also) set with rennet, and brined. It is eaten at breakfast, in salads, menemen and börek, and resembles feta, lighvan and sirene.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

String cheese.text: The US snack cheese: low-moisture part-skim mozzarella that is pulled into strings and peeled apart.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Nabulsi.text: Nabulsi is a brined cheese from Nablus in the West Bank, made mainly from sheep's milk (goat's or cow's also, or a sheep-cow blend called mashmouleh). The pressed curd is boiled and stored in brine flavoured with mastic and mahleb. It is soaked to remove salt before it is used in knafeh.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Erzincan tulum.text: Erzincan tulum is a skin-ripened tulum cheese from Eastern Anatolia, Turkey.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

İzmir tulum.text: İzmir tulum is a skin-ripened tulum cheese of the Aegean region of Turkey, also made in Aydın, Manisa, Muğla and Balıkesir.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Divle.text: Divle is a tulum cheese from Karaman in Central Anatolia, Turkey, also known as Divle Obruk.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Çimi.text: Çimi is a tulum cheese from Akseki in Antalya, Turkey.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Kargı.text: Kargı is a tulum cheese from Çorum on the Black Sea side of Turkey, made at about 25 t a year.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Cotija.text: Cotija is a Mexican cow's-milk cheese from Michoacán. The milk is salted before fermentation, the curd is milled into small pieces, pressed and aged 100–365 days. Young Cotija resembles a mild feta; aged Cotija (añejo) is close to Parmesan.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Kefalotyri.text: Kefalotyri is a hard, salty Greek and Cypriot cheese made from sheep's milk, goat's milk or a mix of the two, white to yellow depending on the milk. It is ripened for about three months or longer, and is eaten as it is, fried in olive oil as saganaki, or grated over dishes and into pies.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Queso Oaxaca.text: Oaxaca cheese, also called quesillo or queso de hebra, is a white, semi-hard Mexican cow's-milk cheese first made in the state of Oaxaca. It is a pasta filata cheese: the curd is stretched into long ribbons that are rolled up like a ball of yarn, and it is stringy like string cheese or mozzarella.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ricotta salata.text: Ricotta salata is ricotta pressed, salted, dried and aged into a firm table or grating cheese. Aged varieties keep for up to a year.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ricotta infornata.text: Ricotta infornata is ricotta baked until it gets a brown, lightly charred crust; it is popular in Sardinia and Sicily.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ricotta affumicata.text: Ricotta affumicata is smoked ricotta, usually smoked over oak or chestnut; a Calabrian version comes from the Sila.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Aralac.text: Aralac was the American casein fibre, developed by the research arm of National Dairy Products from skim-milk casein and marketed around 1940. It was blended with wool, mohair, rayon and fur felt, and milk-protein fibre was no longer made in the US by the end of the 1940s.

QMilch.text: Qmilch is a modern German milk fibre developed by Anke Domaske, made from German dairy waste milk that cannot be sold. The maker says the process is free of harsh chemicals ("so natural you can eat it"), unlike older casein fibres that were hardened with formaldehyde; this rests on the company's own statements.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Erinoid.text: Erinoid was the British name for Galalith casein-formaldehyde plastic: Syrolit Ltd took the UK licence and renamed itself Erinoid Ltd, making it at Dudbridge near Stroud, Gloucestershire.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Lactoid.text: Lactoid is a trade name for casein-formaldehyde plastic, of the Galalith kind.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Aladdinite.text: Aladdinite was the name of Galalith-type casein-formaldehyde plastic in the US.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

fairlife.text: An American brand of ultra-filtered milk owned by Coca-Cola, sold as whole, reduced-fat, fat-free and flavoured milk. It first appeared in Minnesota in February 2014 and went national in February 2015; it is lactose-free and made without added protein powder.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Basundi.text: Basundi is an Indian dessert from Maharashtra and Gujarat made by slowly boiling milk until it is reduced by about half, then sweetening it with sugar, cardamom, charoli or saffron and serving it chilled with nuts.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Palkova.text: Palkova is a sweet of Tamil Nadu made by boiling milk down with sugar to a thick grainy mass; the Srivilliputhur version, from cow milk and sugar only, has a geographical indication.

links.name: Outlook Traveller, Tamil Nadu GI products

sources.text: Written from this source.

Cuajada.text: A creamy, jelly-like milk dessert of northern Spain, especially Navarre and the Basque Country: warm milk set with rennet and eaten with sugar or honey. It was traditionally made with sheep's milk in a clay or wooden bowl; today it is mostly cow's milk.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

So.text: A dairy product made in Japan from the 7th to the 10th century by boiling milk down to a solid; it was paid to the court as tribute, used as medicine and offered to the gods, and daigo was made by processing it further.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Pastillas de leche.text: A Filipino milk sweet whose name means milk pills; it is made from carabao or cow milk (or both) with sugar and calamansi juice and comes from San Miguel, Bulacan.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Yak butter.text: Yak butter is butter made from the milk of the female yak, a staple of Tibet, the Himalaya and Mongolia: eaten with roasted barley flour, churned into butter tea, burned in lamps and modelled into festival sculptures.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Shar tos.text: Mongolian clarified butter, the yellow oil melted gently from tsagaan tos, the white butter made by straining and churning cream.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Manteiga de garrafa.text: A liquid or pasty butterfat from north-east Brazil, made by cooking cream until almost all its water has gone, then decanting and bottling the fat. Brazilian law calls it manteiga da terra, manteiga de garrafa or manteiga do sertao.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Shrikhand.text: Shrikhand is a sweet dish of strained yoghurt, sugar, saffron and cardamom from Gujarat and Maharashtra, chilled and often topped with nuts. The BIS standard calls for at least 58 % total solids.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Sweet lassi.text: Sweet lassi is the sweet form of lassi, a drink of dahi stirred with water and sugar and served chilled, popular in Punjab and Haryana. Fruit such as mango is often blended in.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Juju dhau.text: Juju dhau, 'king of yoghurt' in Nepal Bhasa, is a thick, custard-like sweet curd from Bhaktapur, made by the Newar from boiled, sweetened buffalo milk and set in clay pots.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Sho.text: Sho is the Tibetan word for the yoghurt made from the milk of the dri, the female yak. It is the usual first step of Tibetan butter-making and gives its name to the Shoton yoghurt festival.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Aqit.text: A dried dairy product of the Arabian Bedouin: churned buttermilk is heated until it curdles and the curd is dried into hard discs that keep for months.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Qatiq.text: A fermented milk of the Turkic countries and Bulgaria, a more solid yoghurt than ayran, made from boiled milk left warm for 6-10 hours.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Kivuguto.text: The popular soured milk of Rwanda: raw milk left to sour for two to three days in a smoked wooden jar or gourd, giving a thick, tangy, lightly smoky drink.

Ititu.text: A concentrated sour milk curd of the Borana of southern Ethiopia, built up in a smoked vessel over weeks by adding fresh milk and draining whey.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Amabere amaruranu.text: A fermented milk of the Abagusii people of the Kisii highlands in south-western Kenya, made from boiled cow's milk soured in a gourd.

Hazo.text: A spiced, fermented buttermilk of northern Ethiopia (Tigray): arrera is mixed with pulse or cereal flour and spices and left to ferment for two to three days.

Jocoque.text: A Mexican fermented milk between yoghurt and cheese, soured with lactic cultures and strained until thick; its dry form, jocoque seco, is eaten with tostadas. It came with Lebanese cooking and resembles labneh.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Jocoque seco.text: The dried form of Mexican jocoque: the strained, soured milk is dehydrated into firm curd, similar to Arab labneh, and shaped into 3-4 cm balls that may be kept in olive oil with thyme, dill or mint. Eaten with tostadas.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Suero costeño.text: A viscous, salted, sour milk of Colombia’s Caribbean coast, made from raw milk that sours by itself and eaten with arepas and boiled yuca. Its name is the Spanish word for whey, but it is a soured whole milk.

Beijing yoghurt.text: A traditional sweet fermented milk of Beijing: milk is sweetened, mixed with glutinous-rice wine, poured into small bowls and heated in a special barrel with a central heat chamber, then cooled.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Amasi.text: A thick, curdled, sour fermented milk of southern Africa (also emasi, maas, mafi), eaten in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Lesotho and often compared to cottage cheese or plain yoghurt with a much stronger flavour. Traditionally unpasteurised cow's milk sours in a smoked calabash or skin bag; the watery whey (umlaza) is poured off and the thick curd is amasi.

Kalari.text: Kalari, or kaladi, is a traditional cheese of the Dogra people of Jammu, made around Ramnagar in the Udhampur district from raw full-fat cow or buffalo milk. The curd is packed into small leaf bowls and dried in the sun, so it is dry outside and moist inside, and it is usually fried before eating.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Bandel cheese.text: Bandel cheese is a small round, salted and often smoked unripened cheese from West Bengal, introduced by the Portuguese at Bandel and made today mainly near Kolkata. It is like Surti paneer but made from cow's milk.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Chhena poda.text: Chhena poda, Odia for burnt cheese, is a baked sweet of Odisha made from kneaded chhena, sugar and semolina, browned for several hours so that the sugar caramelises. It is credited to Sudarsan Sahu of Dashapalla after 1947.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Pantua.text: Pantua is a Bengali sweet of deep-fried balls of chhena, semolina, milk and ghee soaked in sugar syrup, from pale brown to nearly black depending on how long it is fried.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Chum chum.text: Chomchom, cham cham or chum chum is a Bengali sweet made from chhena and garnished with coconut or mawa flakes; the oval brown Porabari variety of Tangail district dates from the mid-19th century.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Rasabali.text: Rasabali is a sweet of Odisha: flat palm-sized patties of chhena deep-fried until reddish-brown and soaked in rabri, thickened sweetened milk with cardamom. It began as an offering at the Baladevjew temple in Kendrapara and received a GI tag in October 2023.

Adyghe cheese.text: A mild, crumbly fresh cheese of the North Caucasus made from heated cow milk curdled with sour whey and moulded in baskets; it does not melt when baked or fried.

Dambalkhacho.text: A pungent Georgian cheese from Pshavi and Tianeti: salted curd balls dried by the fire and ripened in sealed clay pots until a mould grows on them.

Klila.text: A very hard, dried cheese of eastern Algeria (and Morocco) made by heating lben until it curdles, draining the curd and drying it in the sun to under 10 % water.

Karish.text: A fresh, soft, white, low-fat Egyptian cheese made by draining laban rayeb (soured skimmed milk) on a mat and salting it lightly.

Queijo de Azeitão.text: A soft, creamy Portuguese sheep's-milk cheese from the Arrábida hills near Setúbal, curdled with cardoon flower instead of animal rennet and ripened about three weeks. Protected designation of origin since 1986.

Dali ni horbo.text: A cheese of the Batak people of Tapanuli, North Sumatra: water buffalo milk is boiled and curdled with pineapple juice or papaya leaf juice.

Litsusu.text: A water buffalo cheese of Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia, set with enzymes from the litsusu tree.

Cologanti.text: A water buffalo cheese of Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia, set with enzymes from the litsusu tree.

Philadelphia.text: An American cream cheese brand, first made in 1872 by William Lawrence of Chester, New York, who tried to make Neufchâtel and added too much cream. It took the Philadelphia name in 1880 with the distributor A. L. Reynolds, and is now owned by Kraft Heinz and Mondelez International.

Tvorog.text: A soft white fresh cheese of Central and Eastern Europe: milk is fermented and the whey is drained off, traditionally in hanging bags. Its fat runs from nil to about 23 %, and unlike German quark it is often made from whole milk.

Magerquark.text: The lean grade of German quark, made from skimmed milk with no cream stirred in, so it holds under 10 % fat in dry matter. Like all quark it is about 80 % water, and the law asks for at least 73 % water in the fat-free mass.

Dry curd cottage cheese.text: Cottage cheese of washed curd grains with no cream dressing, so under 0.5 % milkfat. The US standard of identity allows at most 80 % moisture and requires skimmed-milk ingredients.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Neufchâtel (US).text: A factory-made, unaged cream cheese with about a third less fat and more moisture than regular cream cheese, softer and sold as the reduced-fat choice. It is not the French Neufchâtel, a Normandy PDO cheese ripened under white mould for 8–10 weeks.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Chechil.text: A brined string cheese of Armenia and Georgia, usually made from skimmed cow milk that is soured, set with rennet, scalded and pulled into thin strands that are braided into coils.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Tenili.text: A traditional Georgian string cheese from Meskheti, made from sheep milk, braided in hot whey and matured packed into a clay pot.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Imeruli.text: A young Georgian cheese from Imereti, made from cow milk with up to 20 % buffalo or goat milk, set, scalded, self-pressed in forms and brined for a day.

Guda.text: A sheep-milk cheese from Tusheti in Georgia, salted in layers and ripened in a sheepskin bag; the name means cheese from a bag.
