Lighvan.text: A sour, brined curd cheese traditionally made from raw sheep milk in Lighvan, Iran, without any starter; its acidity comes from the milk's own bacteria.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Jibneh Arabieh.text: A soft white cheese of the Middle East, popular around the Persian Gulf, with a mild taste like feta but less salty; originally from Bedouin goat or sheep milk, now mostly cow milk.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Otlu peynir.text: A semi-hard, salty cheese of the Van province in Turkey, flavoured with wild herbs and matured underground.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Jben.text: A fresh, unripened cheese of Morocco and Algeria, made from raw cow's or goat's milk and traditionally drained in cloth and wrapped in palm leaves in the Rif town of Chefchaouen.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Bouhezza.text: A soft, salty, semi-fat Algerian cheese of the Aurès (Chaouia) region, made from raw goat, sheep or cow milk and ripened for one to six months in a goatskin bag filled with salted lben.

Rumi.text: The main hard cheese of Egypt, made from full-cream cow's or buffalo milk without starter and ripened for several months, when it turns sharp and pungent.

Gibna bayda.text: A soft, white, salty Sudanese cheese pickled in brine or whey, resembling feta; made from cow, goat or sheep milk, usually at home or on small farms.

Mudafara.text: A Sudanese stretched-curd cheese: rennet-set cow's milk curd is scalded in hot water, pulled into threads, braided and stored in brine.

Caravane.text: A soft, Brie-like cheese made from camel's milk in Mauritania by the dairy Tiviski, founded by Nancy Abeiderrahmane; sold mainly in Mauritania and Senegal.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Queijo Canastra.text: A pressed raw-milk cow's cheese from Serra da Canastra in south-west Minas Gerais, Brazil, sold fresh (about 4 days), half-cured or fully cured (about 40 days). Part of the Minas artisanal cheese craft that IPHAN recognised as national heritage in 2008.

Queijo Minas frescal.text: The soft, white, very moist fresh cheese of Brazil, named for Minas Gerais: milk is set with rennet, the raw curd is drained and the cheese is eaten fresh, often with guava paste (Romeu e Julieta).

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Tchoukou.text: A hard, dry cheese of Niger, made by women from raw cow's or goat's milk, set with a spiced rennet, drained and sun-dried on mats.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Queijo de coalho.text: A firm, elastic, mild and slightly acidic cow's-milk cheese of north-east Brazil that squeaks when bitten and browns without melting, so it is grilled on skewers over charcoal. Brazilian law (IN 30/2001) defines it as a cheese sold within about ten days of making.

Queijo de manteiga.text: A soft, buttery, straw-yellow cheese of north-east Brazil: curd made by acidifying milk is washed, melted and enriched with manteiga de garrafa, then moulded. Brazilian law (IN 30/2001) reserves the name for a purely dairy product.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Reggianito.text: An Argentine hard cheese made in 6.8 kg wheels by Italian immigrants as a local answer to Parmigiano Reggiano, ripened about six months and grated over pasta.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Afuega'l pitu.text: A soft, crumbly cow's-milk cheese from central Asturias, set slowly by lactic acid and drained in moulds or cloth. It is eaten fresh or ripened for weeks, white or kneaded with paprika to a red-orange paste. Protected designation of origin.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Queso Chihuahua.text: A soft white Mexican cow's-milk cheese, similar to mild white Cheddar or Monterey Jack, first made by the Mennonite communities of Chihuahua and sold in braids, balls or rounds. It melts well.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Kesong puti.text: A soft, unaged white cheese from the Philippines, made from unskimmed carabao (water buffalo) milk and salt, set with rennet, vinegar or citrus juice and traditionally sold wrapped in banana leaf.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Langtang yak cheese.text: A hard cheese of the Langtang valley in Nepal, made from yak and nak (female yak) milk by the Swiss method that Swiss cheesemakers brought to Kyangjin in the 1950s.

Afyon kaymagi.text: Turkish buffalo-milk kaymak from Afyonkarahisar, a protected geographical indication: a thick cream of at least 60 % fat skimmed from slowly heated, overnight-rested raw buffalo milk.

Double-skin milk.text: A milk dessert from Daliang in Shunde, Guangdong, now eaten across Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Macau: boiled buffalo milk forms a skin as it cools, egg white sets the milk beneath, and a second skin forms after steaming.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

MPC80.text: A milk protein concentrate named for its protein: at least 79.5 % of the powder is milk protein, the rest mostly lactose (under 9 %), ash (under 8 %) and fat (under 2.5 %). Merinova.text: Merinova was one of the trade names of casein wool, the regenerated milk-protein fibre that Antonio Ferretti patented in 1935 and that Snia Viscosa in Italy sold from 1936, like Lanital and Aralac.

Sorke.text: A Levantine spread made by mashing well-aged, fermented shanklish with its mould and herbs into a strong, pungent paste, usually eaten with chopped tomato and onion and olive oil.

Messmör.text: Swedish whey spread: whey boiled down until it caramelises into a soft, brownish spread. Unlike Norwegian prim, no cream or sugar is mentioned.

Getmessmör.text: Messmör made from goat whey instead of cow whey.

Parenica.text: Parenica is a semi-firm, non-ripening, steamed and usually smoked Slovak cheese, wound from strips into snail-like spirals. In the 1800s it was made from pure raw sheep milk; modern versions also use cow milk or mixtures.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Korbáčik.text: Korbáčik, Polish korbacz, is a semi-hard string cheese from the Orava region of Slovakia and southern Poland: steamed cheese pulled into fine threads and interwoven into braids. It comes smoked or unsmoked, from sheep or cow milk.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Žázrivský korbáčik.text: Žázrivský korbáčik is a korbáčik that may be made only in the village of Žázrivá in northern Slovakia. Soured cow milk cheese is steamed, pulled by hand into strands and plaited into the shape of a whip. It is a protected geographical indication product.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Oštiepok.text: Oštiepok is a traditional smoked Slovak sheep milk cheese, protected under the EU PGI. It is shaped like a large egg or cone and decorated with patterns; milk is sheep, sheep plus cow, or cow.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Pule.text: Pule, or magareći sir, is a Serbian cheese made from 60 % Balkan donkey milk and 40 % goat milk at the Zasavica nature reserve. It is crumbly and reported to taste like manchego, and is among the most expensive cheeses because so little milk is available.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Katiki Domokou.text: Katiki Domokou is a soft white cheese from Domokos in Phthiotis, Greece, made from goat and sheep milk. It has PDO status, a low fat content, and is eaten on toast, in salads or in pitas.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Picodon.text: Picodon is a small flat disc of goat milk cheese from the Rhône hills of the Drôme and Ardèche, France. The name means spicy in Occitan; it is soft, unpressed and dry, and loses up to half its weight when aged.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Graviera Kritis.text: Graviera is a Greek hard cheese made in wheels with the crisscross mark of its draining cloth, and is Greece's second most popular cheese after feta. Graviera of Crete is made from sheep milk and has a slightly sweet, burnt caramel flavour.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ladotyri Mytilinis.text: Ladotyri Mytilinis is a hard PDO cheese from Lesbos, Greece, preserved in extra virgin olive oil. It is made from sheep milk or sheep with at most 30 % goat milk and has been produced since ancient times.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ossau-Iraty.text: Ossau-Iraty is a Basque and Béarn cheese made from sheep milk, with AOC status since 1980. It is an uncooked, pressed cheese from the Basco-Béarnaise, Manech red-face and Manech black-face breeds.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Roncal.text: Roncal is a hard, creamy sheep milk cheese made in the seven villages of the Roncal valley in the Navarrese Pyrenees, Spain. It has PDO status and a firm, slightly sharp taste.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Pecorino Sardo.text: Pecorino Sardo is a firm cheese from Sardinia made from the milk of the local Sarda sheep. It has PDO status and comes as dolce, aged 20 to 60 days, and maturo, aged more than 2 months.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Fiore Sardo.text: Fiore Sardo is a hard Sardinian sheep cheese with PDO status, made from raw milk of Sarda ewes set with lamb or kid rennet paste. Wheels are double truncated cones of 1.5 to 4 kg, a table cheese that becomes a grating cheese after six months.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Majorero.text: Majorero is a firm, pale goat milk cheese from the island of Fuerteventura in the Canary Islands, made from the milk of the Majorera goat. It has PDO status and is sold with a natural, oiled, paprika or gofio rind.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ezine.text: Ezine is a full-fat Turkish white cheese from the Ezine district of Çanakkale and the Kaz Dağları, soft to medium-hard and ripened in brine. It is one of the most popular white cheeses in Turkey, with PDO status.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Brânză de burduf.text: Brânză de burduf is a salty Romanian cheese made from sheep, or occasionally buffalo, milk. The matured curd is kneaded with salt and packed into a sheep stomach, a sheep skin or a tube of pine bark.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Renost.text: Renost is the traditional cheese of the Sámi, made from reindeer milk in northern Scandinavia. Historically the curdled milk was poured into a reindeer stomach and hung in the open air; today the few makers use linen cloths, and the cheese turns hard and grainy in the cold and is sometimes smoked.

links.name: Slow Food Ark of Taste, Renost (Reindeer Cheese)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Galotyri.text: Galotyri is a Greek PDO acid-curd, soft spreadable cheese made in Epirus and Thessaly from boiled, naturally acidified ewe milk or ewe and goat milk. It is thick and creamy, with at least 40 % fat in dry matter, at most 75 % moisture and pH 4 to 4.5.

links.name: AIMS Agriculture and Food 2019, Galotyri LAB survey (plus Greek Wikipedia for composition)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Crème Chantilly.text: Whipped cream sweetened with sugar and usually flavoured with vanilla. Its invention is often credited to François Vatel, steward of the Château de Chantilly in the 1660s, which gave it its name.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Spray whipped cream.text: Whipped cream sold in an aerosol can: the cream is charged with nitrous oxide, which dissolves in the butterfat under pressure and foams the cream as it leaves the can.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Devon clotted cream.text: Clotted cream from Devon, the rival of the Cornish in the origin dispute; paler, since the grass has less carotene. In Devon the cream goes on the scone first, in Cornwall the jam.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Three-quarter fat butter.text: An EU legal category of butter with 60-62 % milk fat, below the 80 % of plain butter. It may be sold as reduced-fat or light butter.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Half-fat butter.text: An EU legal category of butter with 39-41 % milk fat. Butter itself must have at least 80 % and under 90 %; anything between the categories is a dairy spread.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Dairy spread.text: A spreadable milk-fat product that falls outside the butter categories: under 39 %, between 41 and 60 %, or between 62 and 80 % milk fat.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Rucava white butter.text: A hand-made Latvian butter (Rucavas baltais sviests) of 39-41 % fat, soft, fluffy and slightly acidic, eaten fresh with boiled potatoes or rye bread. It has a protected geographical indication (2018).

links.name: LSM: No buts, it's Rucava butter

sources.text: Written from this source.

Beurre d'Isigny.text: Butter from the Bay of Veys in Normandy with a protected designation of origin (AOP, PDO since 1996). It can be salted, and can be textured to suit puff pastry; creamy, with hazelnut aromas.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Beurre d'Échiré.text: Butter from cream matured with lactic ferments for 18 hours and churned in wooden churns by the Échiré cooperative in Deux-Sèvres; AOP Charentes-Poitou.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Beurre Rose.text: Cultured milk butter from Luxembourg under the national quality mark, PDO since 2000. The name comes from the pink quality label, not from the butter. Made by continuous churning and tested 15 times a year.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Vologda butter.text: Butter from the Vologda region of Russia, known for a sweet, creamy, nutty flavour. Invented by Nikolai Vereshchagin, who won a gold medal at Paris in 1878 with it as "Parisian butter"; Russia's first protected designation of origin (2010).

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Beurre noir.text: Black butter: a sauce like brown butter, but cooked longer.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Demin 90 (D90).text: NZMP's SureStart Demineralised Whey Powder 90 %: spray-dried, made from cheese whey by precipitation, filtration and ion exchange, for wet and dry blending into infant formula.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Partly demineralised whey.text: Whey with only about 25-30 % of its ash removed, enough for ice cream, bakery and quark, against 90-95 % for infant formula.

links.name: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. 18 Milk and whey fractionation

sources.text: Written from this source.

Follow-on formula.text: Follow-on infant milk formula (FO-IMF), named in the Teagasc/UCC infant-formula thesis as a sibling process of ordinary infant milk formula.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Hydrolysed-protein formula.text: Formula made with hydrolysed proteins; the Teagasc/UCC thesis classes such powders as Type III.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Simplesse.text: The best-known microparticulated whey protein: research began in 1979 at Labatt, it was licensed to NutraSweet in 1984 and trademarked in January 1988. Partial coagulation by heat, a mechanical rather than chemical process.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Rivella.text: Swiss soft drink made with milk serum, launched as Rivella Red in 1952 by Robert Barth with the biologist Hans Süsli. The recipe was first meant for a whey-based beer.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Vivinal GOS.text: The galacto-oligosaccharide ingredient of FrieslandCampina, made from lactose by an enzyme and added to infant formula and other foods to feed gut bifidobacteria.

links.name: NutraIngredients 2025: GOS gains traction in infant milk formulas

sources.text: Written from this source.

MPC70.text: A milk protein concentrate powder of about 70 % protein in dry matter, the middle of the 40 to 90 % MPC range: skimmed milk ultrafiltered to hold back casein and whey proteins while lactose, minerals and water pass, then evaporated and spray dried. More protein and less lactose than MPC35 or MPC50, but short of the diafiltered MPC80 and above.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Black Cow.text: Vodka made in West Dorset since 2012 by Jason Barber and Paul Archard from the whey of cheese milk, distilled to about 48 %, cut to 40 % and filtered three times, once through coconut-husk carbon.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Low-heat skim milk powder.text: Skim milk powder heated only lightly before drying, so most of its whey protein stays undenatured (WPNI above 6.0 mg/g). It is the grade for milk fortification, cottage cheese, cultured skim milk and chocolate milk drinks.

links.name: US Dairy Export Council: Non-fat dry milk and skim milk powder

sources.text: Written from this source.

Medium-heat skim milk powder.text: The middle heat class of skim milk powder (WPNI 1.51-5.99 mg/g), used in prepared mixes, ice cream, confectionery and meat products. The vast majority of skim milk powder is of this class.

links.name: US Dairy Export Council: Non-fat dry milk and skim milk powder

sources.text: Written from this source.

High-heat skim milk powder.text: Skim milk powder heated hardest before drying, so little whey protein is left undenatured (WPNI below 1.50 mg/g). It goes into bakery, meat products and ice cream.

links.name: US Dairy Export Council: Non-fat dry milk and skim milk powder

sources.text: Written from this source.

Instant skim milk powder.text: Skim milk powder that has been agglomerated after spray-drying so that it dissolves in cold water.

links.name: US Dairy Export Council: Non-fat dry milk and skim milk powder

sources.text: Written from this source.

Double-toned milk.text: Toned milk taken one step further: the fat is brought down to a minimum of 1.5 % and the non-fat solids raised to at least 9 %, by blending buffalo or cow milk with skim milk or skim milk powder and water. Sold in India as a cheap low-fat pasteurised milk, for example in pouches.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Valio lactose-free milk.text: Milk from the Finnish dairy cooperative Valio with the lactose removed, developed in 2001 and called the first totally lactose-free milk in the world. Unlike milk treated only with lactase it does not taste sweet.

links.name: Valio: pioneer in lactose free dairy

sources.text: Written from this source.

Minus L.text: Lactose-free UHT milk of the Omira dairy group in Ravensburg, Germany, introduced in 2001 and still sold as MinusL. The classic 1.5 % fat version holds under 0.1 g lactose per 100 g, down from about 4.5 %, because the lactose is split by lactase.

links.name: Dairy Industries International: Milk aimed at the lactose intolerant (24 Sep 2001)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Organic Valley Ultra.text: Line of ultra-filtered organic milk from the US farmer cooperative Organic Valley, launched on 22 July 2019 as the first organic ultra-filtered milk in the US. It has about 50 % more protein and 50 % less sugar than ordinary milk and is lactose-free.

links.name: DairyReporter: Organic Valley debuts new Ultra filtered milk

sources.text: Written from this source.

Speisequark 20 %.text: Quark of the Halbfettstufe: 20 % fat in dry matter, which is a low-fat quark, made by adding some cream to skimmed-milk quark at the end of the process. German shops mainly sell Magerquark, 20 % and 40 % quark.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Sahnequark.text: Quark of the Fettstufe, 40 % fat in dry matter, also called Sahnequark. The fat comes from cream added to skimmed-milk quark at the end of the process; it is one of the two fat grades, with 20 %, that German shops sell besides Magerquark.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Rahmquark.text: Quark of the Rahmstufe: 50 % fat in dry matter, about 10 g fat per 100 g since quark is roughly 80 % water. Cream is added to skimmed-milk quark at the end of the process.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Doppelrahmquark.text: Quark of the Doppelrahmstufe, the richest German grade, with more than 60 % fat in dry matter (German Wikipedia gives 65 to 85 %). Cream is added to skimmed-milk quark at the end of the process.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Long-life quark.text: Quark that is heated after separation to inactivate all microorganisms, so it keeps without a cold chain. Stabilisers are added in the buffer tank before the final heating.

links.name: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, Cheese

sources.text: Written from this source.

Muhallebi.text: A milk pudding of the Middle East made by boiling milk with sugar and thickening it with rice flour, starch or semolina; it was in Arab and Persian cookbooks by the 10th century.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Gammelost.text: Gammelost (gamalost) is a traditional Norwegian cheese, once a staple that kept for long without cooling. It is made from soured skimmed cow milk, is brownish-yellow, firm, moist and coarse, with about 1 % fat and 50 % protein, and is now made in small quantity, mostly by one dairy in Vik.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Pultost.text: Pultost is a soft, mature Norwegian sour milk cheese flavoured with caraway. It is made from soured skimmed milk, salted, and is acid-set and very low in fat; it is spread on bread or flatbread or eaten with boiled potatoes.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Jānu siers.text: Jāņu siers is a Latvian sour milk cheese eaten at the Jāņi midsummer festival. Its curd comes from both soured and fresh cow milk and is cooked with eggs, butter, salt and caraway into a firm cylinder. It has been an EU Traditional Speciality Guaranteed since 2015.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Brousse du Rove.text: Brousse du Rove is a fresh goat cheese from Le Rove near Marseille, made only on the farm from whole milk of the Rove goat breed. It has had a protected designation of origin since 2018 and is traditionally eaten sweetened with orange-flower water.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Caboc.text: Caboc is a Scottish cream cheese made from double cream or cream-enriched milk, formed into a log and rolled in toasted pinhead oatmeal. It is rennet-free, with about 67-69 % fat, and is served with oatcakes. It is said to go back to the 15th century and was a cheese of the wealthy, unlike crowdie.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Double-cream cheese.text: The richer of the two classic kinds of cream cheese: soured and drained from a mix of cream and milk that starts at about 9–11 % fat, which gives a final product with at least 33 % fat. This is the type of Philadelphia-style cream cheese.

links.name: Phadungath 2005, Cream cheese products: A review, Songklanakarin J. Sci. Technol. 27(1)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Single-cream cheese.text: The lighter of the two classic kinds of cream cheese: made from a mix of cream and milk that starts at only about 4.5–5 % fat, so the finished cheese is leaner and moister than double-cream cheese. Both kinds are soured by a mesophilic starter and drained the same way.

links.name: Phadungath 2005, Cream cheese products: A review, Songklanakarin J. Sci. Technol. 27(1)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Paskha.text: Paskha is a festive Easter dish of Eastern Orthodox countries, eaten at the end of Lent. It is made of curd pressed in a mould, in a cooked version with an egg custard and in an uncooked one.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Sernik.text: Polish baked cheesecake made from twaróg curd cheese.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Schabziger.text: Schabziger is a hard, green, strongly flavoured Swiss cheese made only in the canton of Glarus from the Ziger of skimmed milk and powdered blue fenugreek. A Glarus assembly fixed its recipe and origin stamp in 1463, one of the earliest protected brands; today one company, Geska, makes it.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ricotta forte.text: Ricotta forte is a traditional soft, creamy, spicy and slightly bitter cheese of Basilicata and Apulia in southern Italy. Bacteria and yeast ferment the ricotta, which gives it its sharp taste and strong smell. It is on the Italian list of traditional food products (PAT).

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Anari.text: A soft, chalk-white Cypriot whey cheese, usually made from the whey left over from halloumi or kefalotyri with a little goat or sheep milk added. Eaten fresh with carob syrup or honey, or salted and dried hard for grating.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ziger.text: Ziger (Zieger in Germany and Austria) is a Swiss whey cheese: the whey protein is precipitated with acid, alone or with some skimmed milk or buttermilk. It is not aged, and is sold fresh or smoked.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Formaggio di fossa.text: Formaggio di fossa (pit cheese) comes from Sogliano al Rubicone in Emilia-Romagna, where cheese has been buried in pits dug in tufa since the 14th century. Cheese sold as fossa di Sogliano has had protected designation of origin status since 2009.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Montebore.text: Montebore is a raw-milk cheese from the Tortona hills of Piedmont, built from stacked rounds like a tiered cake. It is mentioned in the 12th century, was served at a Sforza wedding in 1489, and had practically died out by 1982 before one old maker taught it to a new generation; it is now a Slow Food Presidium.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Crowdie.text: Crowdie (Gaelic gruth) is a soft, fresh, crumbly Scottish cheese that crofters made from the skim milk left after taking the cream for butter. It is a lactic cheese: the milk sours by itself and the curd is warmed, drained in a cloth and salted, sometimes with a little cream.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Hangop.text: Hangop is a Dutch dessert made from buttermilk or yoghurt that is hung in a cloth to drain overnight, leaving a thick, quark-like mass. It is easy to make at home and is now also made in factories.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Chongos zamoranos.text: Chongos zamoranos is a Mexican dessert of curdled milk, made with rennet tablets, milk, sugar and cinnamon. The result is soft cheese-like curd in a sweet brown milky syrup; its origin is attributed to convents in Zamora, Michoacán, in the colonial period.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ostkaka.text: Ostkaka is a Swedish curd cake from Hälsingland and Småland, traditionally made from raw milk and rennet. The set curd is drained, baked, and eaten tepid with jam, cloudberries and cream.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Pastry cream.text: Thick custard stabilised with starch, used to fill éclairs, tarts and cakes.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Crème caramel.text: A baked egg custard set over a layer of soft caramel and turned out of its mould.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Crème brûlée.text: A rich custard topped with a crisp layer of burnt sugar, served slightly chilled.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Crema catalana.text: A Catalan custard of milk, egg yolks and sugar with a burnt-sugar crust.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Leche flan.text: The Philippine version of flan: a firm caramel-topped egg custard.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Natillas.text: A Spanish custard of milk and eggs, thinner than flan and without caramel.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Fudge.text: A soft confection of sugar, butter and milk, beaten as it cools so the sugar forms fine crystals.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Booza.text: A frozen dairy dessert from the Levant, pounded and stretched rather than churned, so it is chewy and stretchy.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Bastani.text: Iranian ice cream of milk, egg yolk, sugar, rose water, saffron and pistachios, often with flakes of frozen clotted cream.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Semifreddo.text: An Italian frozen dessert of whipped cream, egg whites and sugar, frozen in a mould for a light, mousse-like texture.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Blancmange.text: A sweet European dessert of milk or cream, sugar and a thickener, usually set in a mould and served cold.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Tavuk göğsü.text: A Turkish milk pudding made with shredded chicken breast.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Kazandibi.text: A Turkish dessert, a milk pudding whose bottom is caramelised in the pan, from the Ottoman palace kitchens.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Vla.text: A Dutch custard-like milk dessert sold in cartons, in vanilla, chocolate and other flavours.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Semolina pudding.text: Porridge-like pudding of semolina cooked in milk, served with sugar, cinnamon, fruit or syrup.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Sütlaç.text: Turkish rice pudding of milk, rice and sugar, often baked in clay dishes.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Arroz con leche.text: The Spanish and Latin American rice pudding, usually flavoured with cinnamon.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Arroz doce.text: The Portuguese and Brazilian sweet rice pudding.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Mathura peda.text: The original peda, from Mathura in Uttar Pradesh: thick, semi-soft brown balls of khoa, sugar and cardamom.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Dharwad peda.text: A peda from Dharwad in Karnataka, made from the milk of Dharwadi buffaloes heated and stirred continuously with sugar; it has GI tag number 80.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Khurchan.text: A North Indian winter sweet of scraped layers of cream skin from simmering milk, sweetened.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Sgushchyonka.text: The Russian name for condensed milk; sweetened whole condensed milk is made to a GOST standard.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Varenaya sgushchyonka.text: Condensed milk cooked until it browns, eaten as a spread and filling in Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.

sources.text: Written from this source.

Milk protein isolate (MPI).text: The most protein-rich milk protein powder: skim milk ultrafiltered and diafiltered until at least 89.5 % of the powder (ADPI definition; commonly sold as 90 % or more) is milk protein, with casein and whey proteins still in roughly their milk ratio. It cannot be made by mixing separately produced caseinate and whey protein. Used to fortify high-protein bars and heat-treated (UHT) drinks.

links.name: American Dairy Products Institute: Milk protein isolate (MPI)

sources.text: Written from this source.

Importal.text: A lactitol laxative sold as a powder in 10 g sachets that is dissolved in water; in France it is licensed for the symptomatic treatment of constipation and for hepatic encephalopathy. The marketing authorisation holder in France is Angelini Pharma (Rome), distributed by SERB. Wikipedia lists it as the trade name of lactitol in Europe.

links.name: Vidal: Importal 10 g, poudre pour solution buvable en sachet

sources.text: Written from this source.

Pizensy.text: The US brand of lactitol, a powder for solution taken as an osmotic laxative for chronic idiopathic constipation in adults, approved in February 2020.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Iowa State Fair butter cow.text: A life-size cow sculpted in butter at the Iowa State Fair every year since 1911; the first was made by John K. Daniels, sponsored by Beatrice Creamery.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Tibetan torma.text: A temporary altar offering of Tibetan Buddhism, made of butter (ideally yak butter), dyed, often with flour and milk, shaped at Tibetan New Year.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Butter lamp.text: A lamp that burns butter, in Tibetan Buddhism clarified yak butter, now often vegetable oil.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Chocolate milk.text: Milk with cocoa and sugar; the commonest flavoured milk.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Horlicks.text: British-American malted milk powder for a hot drink, first sold as an infant and invalid food. The brand began with the Horlick brothers in Chicago in 1873.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Ovaltine.text: Malt-based drink powder invented by the Swiss pharmacist Albert Wander in Bern in 1904 and sold as Ovomaltine in Switzerland.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Milo.text: Malted chocolate drink powder created by Thomas Mayne at Nestlé in Australia in 1934, made of malted barley, milk powder, cocoa and sugar.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Viking Melk.text: Norwegian evaporated milk in a tin, developed by Olav Johan Sopp in 1891 and sold under the Viking Melk name by Nestlé since 1897.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Carnation.text: American evaporated milk brand, now Nestlé’s; the first Carnation plant opened in Kent, Washington, in 1899.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

PET.text: American evaporated milk brand now owned by Smucker’s.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Matka kulfi.text: Kulfi frozen in a matka, an earthen pot kept cold with ice and salt. Sold by kulfiwallahs, the street vendors, and said to give a smooth texture without ice crystals.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Kulfi falooda.text: A scoop or slice of kulfi served over falooda, thin vermicelli noodles, often with rose syrup. Served this way it is a dessert plate rather than a different kind of kulfi.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Beijinho.text: Brazilian party sweet, a brigadeiro made with coconut instead of cocoa and rolled in sugar. Its name means "little kiss".

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Brigadeiro de colher.text: Spoon brigadeiro: the brigadeiro mixture served soft in a small container and eaten with a spoon instead of being rolled into balls.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Dois amores.text: Brigadeiro combining dark chocolate and white chocolate.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Eagle Brand.text: American sweetened condensed milk from Gail Borden's company, sold under the Eagle Brand name by 1858.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Milchmädchen.text: Nestlé's Swiss sweetened condensed milk, the best known tin in Germany.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

La Lechera.text: The Mexican version of Nestlé's Milchmädchen tin.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Gala Peter.text: The first milk chocolate sold for eating, made by Daniel Peter of Vevey from 1887 (he had solved the problem in 1875 using condensed milk from his neighbour Henri Nestlé).

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Cadbury Dairy Milk.text: British milk chocolate bar launched in 1905 by George Cadbury Jr, made with milk crumb; the UK's best-selling bar in 2014.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Hershey bar.text: American milk chocolate bar introduced by Milton Hershey in 1900, made by a secret process rather than by crumb.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.

Pinkberry.text: California frozen yoghurt chain opened in West Hollywood in January 2005 that revived the 1980s frozen yoghurt craze; customers choose toppings.

Malted milkshake.text: A milkshake made with malted milk powder, called a malt.

Bogurar doi.text: Sweet doi from Bogura in northern Bangladesh, sold in earthen pots; it received a Geographical Indication tag. Bogura makes about 50 tonnes a day in around 400 factories, per the Financial Express.

Bhapa doi.text: Bengali steamed yoghurt dessert: thick hung curd is mixed with sweetened condensed milk, cardamom and often saffron, steamed in small bowls for about 20 minutes and chilled until it sets like a soft cheesecake. Traditional versions sweeten with nolen gur, date-palm jaggery.
